summary: Defines cipher suites, signature schemes, and key exchange mechanisms that use the Russian GOST cryptographic standards with TLS 1.3, and a profile for interoperable implementations. It is informational and exists to make these algorithms available to the Internet community.

eli5.summary: Secure web connections can use different secret-code tools. This document adds a set of codes from Russia's standards to the TLS toolbox.

questions: how to use russian cryptography in tls
how to use gost with tls 1.3
subtitle: Russian cryptographic standards for secure web connections.

tldr.problem: The Internet uses TLS for secure connections, but TLS traditionally relies on Western cryptographic algorithms. Organizations using Russian GOST standards needed a way to integrate them into modern TLS 1.3.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines four cipher suites and seven signature schemes that use Russian cryptographic standards (GOST algorithms) with TLS 1.3, along with key exchange mechanisms and a profile for interoperable implementations.
tldr.outcome: The document is informational and not endorsed by the IETF, making these cipher suites available to the Internet community without guaranteeing their adoption or security standards approval.

today: RFC 9367 remains an Informational RFC that makes Russian GOST cryptographic standards available within TLS 1.3. It has not been updated or obsoleted since its publication in February 2023. The document is not part of the IETF standards track and carries no endorsement from the IETF regarding the security or suitability of GOST algorithms.

sections.title: Overview of GOST Cipher Suites
sections.content:
RFC 9367 extends TLS 1.3 with GOST cipher suites, which implement Russian cryptographic standards. The document defines four cipher suites for record protection and seven signature schemes for authentication, all based on three Russian standards: GOST R 34.12-2015 (block ciphers Kuznyechik and Magma), GOST R 34.11-2012 (hashing), and GOST R 34.10-2012 (digital signatures).

The RFC is informational and explicitly states that the IETF has not endorsed these cipher suites or their security properties. It exists to make Russian cryptographic standards available to the Internet community.
sections.eli5: TLS helps keep web connections secret. This adds Russian cryptographic tools so organizations using Russian standards can also have secure connections.

sections.title: Cipher Suites and Record Protection
sections.content:
The RFC defines four cipher suites with names like TLS_GOSTR341112_256_WITH_KUZNYECHIK_MGM_L. Each cipher suite combines two components: a record protection algorithm and a hash algorithm.

Record protection uses AEAD encryption (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) built from either Kuznyechik (16-byte blocks, 32-byte keys) or Magma (8-byte blocks, 32-byte keys) in Multilinear Galois Mode (MGM). A novel feature is TLSTREE, an external re-keying function that derives a new encryption key for each record based on the sequence number, limiting the amount of data encrypted under a single key. The four suites split into "_L" (light) and "_S" (strong) variants, which differ in how many records can be sent before requiring key changes.

All suites use GOST R 34.11-2012 as the hash algorithm, a Russian standard that produces a 32-byte hash.
sections.eli5: The cipher suite picks the secret code and hashing tool. Kuznyechik and Magma are the code tools, and they change keys often to stay secure. The light and strong versions use different numbers of messages before changing keys.

sections.title: Signature Schemes and Key Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven signature schemes, each combining the GOST R 34.10-2012 signature algorithm with a specific elliptic curve. The 256-bit variants (gostr34102012_256a through 256d) use 32-byte keys and four different elliptic curves; the 512-bit variants (512a through 512c) use 64-byte keys and three curves. These signature schemes are used during the TLS handshake to authenticate the server and optionally the client.

For key exchange, the profile supports three modes: ECDHE (Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman), PSK-only (Pre-Shared Key), and PSK with ECDHE. ECDHE uses seven elliptic curves and is the recommended method. The shared secret is calculated by performing elliptic-curve scalar multiplication and extracting the X-coordinate in little-endian format.
sections.eli5: Before talking, two sides need to prove who they are (signatures) and agree on a secret (key exchange). Signatures use Russian math, and the secret can be made from shared knowledge or by working out a new secret together.

sections.title: TLS 1.3 Handshake Profile
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how GOST algorithms fit into the TLS 1.3 handshake. The ClientHello message MUST include the GOST cipher suites and signature scheme preferences. If using ECDHE, it MUST include one of the seven elliptic curves in the supported_groups extension. The ServerHello chooses one of the offered cipher suites and one of the curves.

Authentication messages (CertificateRequest, Certificate, and CertificateVerify) are modified slightly: the SIGN function wraps the GOST R 34.10-2012 signature by concatenating the r and s values in little-endian format. Certificates must be signed with one of the GOST signature schemes. The RFC emphasizes that external Pre-Shared Keys (PSKs) should only be used in conjunction with mutual authentication for security.
sections.eli5: When client and server start talking, they exchange messages that say which Russian tools they want to use. The server picks one, and they both prove who they are using Russian signatures.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Notes
sections.content:
The RFC contains one key security recommendation: when using TLSTREE for external re-keying, the key derivation functions should only be called when necessary (when the record sequence number changes bits that trigger re-keying). Otherwise, the previous key should be reused. This prevents unnecessary cryptographic operations and reduces side-channel attack surfaces.

Notably, the RFC is non-normative regarding the security of GOST algorithms themselves. It provides no analysis of GOST cryptographic strength, making no claim that these algorithms meet any particular security level. Implementations using these cipher suites are responsible for assessing the suitability of GOST algorithms for their security requirements. The document was published in February 2023 as an Informational RFC by an independent submission, not as part of the IETF standards track.
sections.eli5: When changing keys, skip unnecessary work to avoid mistakes. The document does not promise that Russian codes are as safe as other codes—users must decide if they are right for their needs.
